head: b223ef0352cf4cc0c6d75fe781d83c8226e7d2f8
title: Fix a potential race condition during PTE read/write operations
body:
KernMiri reports a data race: when a `CursorMut` write to a PTE, there may be a concurrent read operation to the same PTE during the `Cursor::new()`. 

For the `read` operation in `Cursor::new()`, reading the PTE either before the write or after the write does not affect correct execution. However, if it reads a PTE that is halfway through being written, it may cause issues. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that the `read`/`write` operations here are at least single instructions. This PR replaces the original `read`/`write` with the `read_once`/`write_once` API to strengthen this guarantee.

title: Enable RCU to read reference to stored pointers
body:
This PR wants to address two limitations of RCU usages: 
1. Make RCU can obtain the reference to `P`. In this way users are able to invoke the methods of `P` like `Arc::clone`.
2. Make RCU manages `NonNullPtr` instead of `OwnerPtr`. Once RCU is used to obtain a reference to `P` instead of `P::target`, the requirement for `P` to be an owning pointer is eliminated. This allows RCU to manage a wider range of pointers, such as `Weak<T>`.

head: e1163681edd747b352745b9dfeaf333f2be7c71b
title: Optimize the usage of `FsResolver` during initialization
body:
This PR is to pave the way for future mount namespace support.

## Include the VDSO library directly

This commit embeds the VDSO library directly into the kernel using include_bytes!. However, since the VDSO library is currently cloned from github during initramfs creation, the current implementation is somewhat inelegant—I'm unsure if this is acceptable as a temporary solution.

**Alternative**: Like the next commit, move the initialization of VDSO to the init task and remain the `FsResolver` usage.

The CI failure is due to the arch-unaware `make check`, #2349 will fix this problem.

## Optimize the `FsResolver` acquisitions during the initialization phase

This commit removes the `ext2` and `exfat` mount operations during kernel boot, delegating them to userspace. It also relocates the logic for building the initramfs file tree and mounting `/dev` into the init task.

The reason for not fully offloading `/dev` mounting to userspace is that the current operations here are relatively complex, and Linux also supports kernel-managed `/dev` mounting and initialization (by enabling `CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT`). Hence retaining these operations remains reasonable.

head: 5f52dd539c0b6b5bd769d4fee3033f68cb09ec52
title: Make the mount-related fields in statx effective
body:
When debugging systemd in nixos, I found that after entering the shell, the `/run/current-system` symlink we prepared in the initialization script could no longer be found, which prevented the `$PATH` environment variable from correctly locating `/run/current-system/sw/bin`. The underlying reason is that systemd automatically mounts a tmpfs at `/run`, overwriting the original contents. In fact, before mounting, systemd will use the `statx` syscall to check if the current path is already a mount root. If it is, it skips the corresponding operation.

In our current `statx` implementation, the `stx_attributes_mask` includes `STATX_ATTR_MOUNT_ROOT`, which implies that the current `stx_attributes` supports the `STATX_ATTR_MOUNT_ROOT` flag. But in reality, we don't actually support this feature, which caused systemd to mistakenly believe that the current path was not a mount root. This PR fixes that issue.

head: d57cfdfad02e9cae75874412c0df06986938a377
title: float: Fix panic at max exponential precision
body:
Rust's formatting machinery allows precision values of up to u16::MAX. Exponential formatting works out the number of significant digits to use by adding one (for the integral digit before the decimal point).

This previously used usize precision, so the maximum validated precision did not overflow, but in commit fb9ce0297682 ("Limit formatting width and precision to 16 bits.") the precision type was narrowed to u16 without widening that addition first.

As a result an exponential precision value of 65535 is no longer handled correctly, because the digit count wraps to 0, and thus "{:.65535e}" panics in flt2dec::to_exact_exp_str with "assertion failed: ndigits > 0". Other formats (and the parser) accept values up to u16::MAX.

A naive fix would be to widen that addition back to usize, but that still does not properly address 16-bit targets, where usize is only guaranteed to be able to represent values up to u16::MAX. The real issue is that this internal API is expressed in the wrong units for the formatter.

Fix this by changing exact exponential formatting to take fractional digits internally as well, and compute the temporary significant digit bound only when sizing the scratch buffer. To support that let's also make formatted length accounting saturate so that extremely large rendered outputs do not reintroduce overflows in padding logic.

This preserves the existing intent and keeps FormattingOptions compact while making formatting work consistently again.

This PR tries to fix the issue rust-lang/rust#164904 and rust-lang/rust#165076. I open a topic in Zulipchat: [Soundness issue about Pattern and Search](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/219381-t-libs/topic/Soundness.20issue.20about.20Pattern.20and.20Search/with/638725746).

In particularly, I think `Pattern` need to ensure that `[into_searcher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/trait.Pattern.html#tymethod.into_searcher)` does return the searcher that search pattern for the given string.

head: db4e9441fb5d019e22100548ae1a1de462565038
title: Fix the behavior of syncing `BlockGroup` metadata in ext2
body:
During debugging NixOS in Asterinas, when creating a file in the ext2 filesystem and then shutting down the system, the file cannot be read correctly upon reboot. The root cause is an issue with the sync operation of ext2's `BlockGroup`. The current implementation directly writes the `IdAlloc` as bytes, but the length of the slice after `as_bytes` does not meet the alignment requirement with `SECTOR_SIZE` specified in `write_bytes_async`, preventing the write operation from proceeding. 

This PR fixes the problem by ensuring the size of `IdAlloc` is aligned with `SECTOR_SIZE` when loading.

head: 1aec7970aa7e8d01a1adbe9d0671e41fd0d619d2
title: Introduce a cache mechanism for `FsType`
body:
Currently, every time we mount a device, we create a new file system instance. However, having multiple file system instances for the same device means each instance has its own independent locks, and these instances could concurrently modify the contents of the device.

This PR addresses the above situation. With this PR, when the same device is mounted multiple times in different locations, these mount instances can actually share the same file system instance, which is aligned with Linux.

head: 81eaaca313dd128905a2b0d3a1e9a607a24c2d5e
title: syscall: chown: enforce CAP_CHOWN and clear the set-ID bits
body:
### The problem

`chown(2)` and its family accept anything from anyone.  `sys_fchown()` and
`sys_fchownat()` forward the request to `Path::set_owner()`/`set_group()`
directly, with no permission check, and nothing clears the set-user-ID or
set-group-ID bits of the file afterwards.

Both are absent on Linux:

* an unprivileged user can hand any file it owns to an arbitrary uid.
  Measured on the same seed image as uid 1000:
  `chown("d1/a_rw", 1001, 1001)` returns `EPERM` on Linux and `0` here;
* because the set-ID bits survive the chown, a user can `chmod u+s` its own
  binary and give it to root, leaving behind a root-owned set-user-ID binary.

### The fix

New `do_chown()`, mirroring Linux's `chown_ok()`/`chgrp_ok()`,
`setattr_should_drop_sgid()` and `setattr_prepare()`:

* changing the owner requires `CAP_CHOWN`; the only exception is a no-op by
  the file's owner;
* changing the group requires `CAP_CHOWN` too, except that the owner of the
  file may keep the group or move it to one of its groups;
* a successful chown of a non-directory clears `S_ISUID`, and clears
  `S_ISGID` too unless the file is not group-executable and the caller is in
  the file's group or has `CAP_FSETID` (directories keep both bits, where
  `S_ISGID` only controls the group of newly created children);
* the stripping is a mode change, so it also requires the owner or
  `CAP_FOWNER`, and it happens even for a `chown(-1, -1)` call;
* the whole request is checked *before* anything is written, so a rejected
  call leaves the file untouched;
* `on_attr_change()` is notified, as `chmod` does since #3864.

The capability plumbing follows the existing `ctx`-based call sites
(`lsm_hooks::on_capable` + `CapableContext::new`, as in
`capable_modify_file_cap()`); `CapSet::CHOWN`, `CapSet::FSETID` and
`CapSet::FOWNER` already exist.

### Notes

* The stripping deliberately does not reuse `xattr.rs::clear_set_id_bits()`:
  that helper implements the content-change rule
  (`setattr_should_drop_suidgid()`, where `CAP_FSETID` preserves both bits),
  which is not what `chown` follows.
* Removing the `security.capability` xattr on chown (`ATTR_KILL_PRIV`) is not
  implemented, so `ChownTest.ChownRemovesSecurityCapability` stays
  blocklisted.
* Like the existing `chmod` path, the owner, group and mode updates are
  separate inode operations, so unlike Linux's single `notify_change()` they
  are not serialized against concurrent updates.  The permission checks
  themselves are complete before the first write.

### Testing

* The rules were checked against a real Linux 7.2-rc5 kernel in a QEMU VM,
  including root and unprivileged callers, no-op and real changes, non-owner
  callers, `CAP_CHOWN` without `CAP_FOWNER`, `chown(-1, -1)`, and
  group-executable / non-group-executable setgid files.  The implementation
  reproduces the kernel's results in all cases.
* The second commit un-blocks the six
  `ChownKinds/ChownParamTest.ChownFilePermissionDenied` cases in the gVisor
  conformance suite, which expect exactly the `EPERM` that this commit adds.
* The patch is formatted with the pinned `rustfmt` (nightly-2026-07-21).
  CI runs the full build and conformance suites.

- `memory::map_frame_range`: A convenience function that creates a new memory mapping by allocating specific frames from physical memory.
- `memory::map_mmio_range`: A convenience function that creates a new memory mapping by allocating specific frames from physical memory with [`MMIO_FLAGS`] as flags.
- `pci::pci_map_bar_mem` as a clean replacement for `allocate_device_register_memory`, even though it's also unused. Maps device memory specified by a Base Address Register.

`gic` & `serial_port_basic` were also modified so that they use `memory::map_mmio_range`.

head: fcb9b8a69ddfacf4c1ea71147bc7e6916d159577
title: `pci` improvements
body:
This reduces the number of exposed `pci` internals:
- All internal consts are now private.
- `pci_read_*` internal methods are now private as well.
- MSI-X mapping and configuration is now done via `PciDevice::pci_mem_map_msix`. Related structs (`MsixVectorEntry` & `MsixVectorTable`) were moved to `pci`, and there is now a `configure` method in `MsixVectorEntry`.
- The `PciDevice::pci_get_interrupt_line` getter was added.
- `nic_queues::{RxQueue, TxQueue}` now use `OptionalCpuId` instead of `Option<u8>`.

This depends on :
- commits from #957
- items added in #948 (`interrupts::InterruptNumber`)

Consequently, CI will fail at least until `interrupts::InterruptNumber` exists.
Quick fix for testing: Add
```rust
pub use core::primitive::u8 as InterruptNumber;
```
to `interrupts::x86_64`.

head: f1fbdae741ffa4bb34192d31d8e7bd9f37ca871d
title: Port `upd` to new `net` API
body:
Ports `upd` (and by extension `ota_update_client` and `http_client`) to the new `net` API.

A couple of points:
- Currently `net::get_ephemeral_port` doesn't keep track of used ports, but that's no better than it was before. I'll leave that for a future PR when I have a better idea of what information we need to track about ports.
- The `LockedSocket::connect` method is a temporary fix until we introduce our own socket types. After this PR I'll have a look at the API `net` needs to expose to `std` and rework our socket abstractions to better reflect this.
- I changed the logic in `ota_update_client` to not reconnect on every loop iteration. Previously, it would open a new connection for every file, but only waited on the last connection. Now it only opens one connection and waits on that connection.
- I'm not sure how I can test the changes to `upd`.

Next steps are:
- Remove `network_manager` and `ethernet_smoltcp_device`
- Tweak `net` interface to better reflect usage patterns and `std` needs
- Track used ports

head: 68c618e56d4615a37fa6bd136d9ce5199761ceb6
title: Port of the `pci` crate
body:
This brings the following changes:
- `pci::scan_pci` maps the pci config space on aarch64, in addition to what it used to do.
- `pci::PciLocation` was modified so that it uses the mapping on aarch64
- `device_manager` calls it (via pci_device_iter) on both platforms
- I tried converting the `const` offsets to an enum but the capability "linked-list" from `find_pci_capability` needs the offset to be a raw u8, and I might also need custom offsets for USB support so I dropped this.
- `QEMU_FLAGS` starts the virt machine with new options: `highmem=on` & `highmem-mmio=on` because without them, the PCI configuration space lies in "low memory" but its base address points to a bunch of zeros for some reason.

Note: while `pci` currently uses port-io on x86 and mmio on aarch64, x86 may also support memory-based PCI configuration in the future; port-io is the legacy way to access the config space.
